Javed Khan Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory Of Columbia University, Palisades, New York Neil D. Opdyke Department of Geology, University of Florida, Gainesville R. A. K. Tahirkheli Centre of Excellence in Geology, University Of Peshwar, Peshawar, Pakistan Abstract. Nine stratigraphic sections in the Siwalik Group, three from the Bhittani Range, five from the Marwat Range, and one from the Khasor Range, were measured and sampled for magnetostratigraphic studies. Progressive alternating field and partial thermal demagnetization of samples indicated the presence of two components of magnetization. These are a secondary component of low coercivity, which can be removed by alternating field demagnetization in fields up to 40 mT and/or temperatures to 400ø6, and a stable primary component of magnetization which has blocking temperatures above 450øC. Therefore all samples were subjected to blanket demagnetization at 450øC and 500øC, and some to temperatures up to 600øC. Positive fold tests from the Bhittani and Marwat ranges indicate the successful isolation of a prefolding characteristic direction of magnetization. A magnetic polarity reversal sequence for ea

s from the Marwat and Khassor ranges are shown in Figure 1. The number of sites sampled and the stratigraphic thickness measured and sampled are given in Table 1. The intensity and direction of remanant magnetization were measured using a Digico spinner magnetometer developed by Molyneaux [1971]. The intensity of natural remnant magnetization ( M) of sa[g_ ples, collected from all of the sections, ranged from 1 x 101- to 5 x 10 - A/m. 3.1. Alternating Field Demagnetization After measuring the NRM, samples were selected for progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization in steps of 5 mT, up to 80 mT (Figure 2). The results of AF demagnetization suggest that the NRM of most of the samples consists of two components of magnetization: low-coercivity component which is removed by AF treatment of up to 40 mT, and a high coercivity component which is not much affected even after treatment to 80 roT. The low-coercivity component is interpreted as a secondary component of magnetization acquired in the Earth's present-day magnetic field. The high-coercivity component does not show significant change in direction or loss of intensity in fields above 25 mT. The more highly coercive rocks are red or brown in color, dearly indicating the presence of hematite. Table 2. Directions of Re

equence consists of a lower red day zone and the upper light gray sandstones. The middle and upper part of the Siwalik Group display only a few siltstone units, each 2 to 5 m thick. Six sites from the Bain Pass A section were also included in this analysis because of overlaps between the sections. The correlation of these two sections was made by tracing a prominent sandstone laterally along strike. Fifty-six sites were sample through 2200 m of the Garhi Landa section. This study and others which followed it opened a new era in tectonics and stratigraphy. The paper presented here utilizes the magnetic time scale pioneered by those authors and is similar to a host of others that have revolutionized the geochronology of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic. It is with great sadness that we submit this paper to a volume commemorating the late Allan Cox. His impact on earth science is profound and will not be forgotten. The Siwalik Group unconformably overlies the Mesozoic rocks and forms the outer part of the anticline. The Siwalik sediments are exposed only along the northwestern flank of the fold. 2. All of these flows are horizontal and are relatively unaltered in thin section. These rocks possess a stable magnetization which is believed to be primary. Samples from 48 lava flows were col- lected from sites located within the Khorat Plateau, the Chao Phraya-Phitsanulok Basin, and the mountainous terrane west of the Chao Phraya-Phitsanulok Basin. These data were combined with previously reported late Neogene data from five flows from western Thailand. Although the average inchnation from the 53 sites is indistiguishable from the expected dipole inchnation, the average declination has a net clockwise rotation of 13.5 0 -4-5.8 0 from the geocentric dipole field. Furthermore, the mean declination values from the 29 flows from the Khorat Plateau are indistinguishable from the present dipole fiel

ed from central and western Thailand are deflected significantly clockwise (Din = 24.4 0 q_7.7 0) from the geocentric dipole field direction. The dif- ferential rotation between western and central Thailand versus the Khorat Plateau suggests that Indochina is composed of at least two structural blocks which underwent a different rotational history. These observations, when combined with geologic and geophysical data from the Chao Phraya-Phitsanulok Basin, Gulf of Thailand, and the intermontane basins of western Thailand, suggest that the rotations are recording a late Neogene phase of E-W extension of these basins. We suggest that the formation of these basins and the related basaltic volcanism developed in reponse to subduction of the Indian plate under western Burma. We envision the tectonics of this region is similar in style to the Basin and Range region of the western United States. More than 250 oriented core samples were drilled during the last five years from a wide variety of rapakivi types in order to determine the direction of the remanent magnetization in the rocks belonging to the Wiborg massif (Wahl, 1925) and its satellites. Most of these rocks were, however, too weakly magnetized to be measured with the fluxgate spinner magnetometer available or were too unstable to give any reliable results. Some rock types, like the dark, sometimes fayalite containing variety, »tirilite» (Wahl, 1925), has a fairly stable component of magnet- ization which is subparallel to the present geo- magnetic field. This magnetization is assumed to be caused by a late chemical remanence asso- ciated with the intense weathering so typical for rapakivi granites. Finally, quartz (granite) porphyre dikes were also sampled. These dikes are known to be genetically and spatially connected with the rapa- 196 K. J. Neuvonen kivi granits. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) found in these samples is weak but quite stable. The fine grained, chilled margins carry the strongest remanence. ally. Biotite occurs as clusters which in some cases can be assumed to be old phenocrysts. The rock has accordingly and with good reason been called granite porphyry (e.g. Savolahti 1956). In many dikes, however, biotite is met only as a ground- mass mineral. Most of the dikes run roughly in SE-NW direction, are 1—30 meters wide, and have a chilled, fine grained contact zone which occurs also against the rapakivi granite. The groundmass consists of potassium feld- spar, quartz and plagioclase. In addition there are biotite and frequently some fluorite and apatite. The remanence is carried by magnetite as indicated by thermal and AF demagnetization. Magnetite is met as fine laths within the biotite clusters, as small needles in the groundmass or some times as large euhedral crystals in which the ilmenite lamells have changed into a mixture of sphene and limonite (goethite). All these mag- netite types are assumed to be of the same age. Evidently, to some extent, a component of the remanent magnetization is carried also by the hydrous iron oxide pigment quite abundant in some samples. d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. They are considered to be correlative with the Calmer basalts [Strong et al., 1978b]. They occur on the beach east and west of Famine Back Cove, with an exposed thickness of 15 m. They were sampled through their thickness over a distance of 1 km. The magnetization of three cores is univectorial (Figures 5 and 6). It remains little changed in alternating fields up to 100 mT and temperatures up to 650øC, and it points to the southeast with intermediate downward inclination. The basalts have un- dergone intense deuteric alteration and hematite is the main carrier of the magnetization. In nine cores there is also a substantial (PEF) component, aligned close to the present earth's field, that is removed at low temperatures or after treatment in low alternating fields. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. The remaining three cores have not only PEF and SE magnetizations, but also very small magnetizations sometimes pointing south sometimes north. These very small components could not be accurately isolated (Figure 7). The northerly ones could be overprints acquired at the time of intrusion of the St. Lawrence Granite (see

d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. N points north with an intermediate upward inclination (declination, 005 ø' incli- nation, -50 ø' alpha (95), 10 ø' paleopole 12øN, 120øE). We consider N to have been acquired close to the time of initial cooling. The H magnetization points south with low inclination. H is also the dominant magnetization in the nearby Permo-Carboniferous Spanish Room Formation. H is considered to be an overprint acquired chemically during the Kiaman Reversed Superchron (Late Carboniferous and Per- mian). The N magnetization corresponds to a paleolatitude of 31 + 7øS, very different from the near- equatorial values expected from the commonly accepted Late Devonian and earliest Carboniferous (Tournaisian) reference paleofields for cratonic North America. This is generally consi

- Carboniferous. The low grade of the metamorphism and the high stability of the magnetizations would suggest that the magnetizations are late Precambrian, but this is by no means certain. The declinations of the Garnish red sandstone (151 ø ) and the Famine Back Cove basalts (133 ø ) are roughly similar, but that of the Calmer mudstone (282 ø) is different, the mag- netization pointing west rather than southeast. Such differ- ences in declination are common indicators of regional shear in orogenic belts [Beck, 1976], and presumably reflect rotation around vertical axes, which occurred possibly in the Acadian orogeny. Precambrian paleopoles in the age range 600-620 Ma are not available from the Canadian Shield [Roy, 1983] so no comparisons can be made with results from the Burin Penin- sula. Late Precambrian rocks of the Avalon Zone resemble those of the Moroccan Meseta, and it has been suggested that they were formerly in close proximity [Schenk, 1972; Strong, 1978]. Paleomagnetic evidence, summarized by Morel [1981], indicates that northwest Africa at about 600 Ma was close to the paleopole. dies show small departures of only a few degrees (with one exception based on limited sampling and two from the Colorado Plateau which may have been rotated) which could be caused by experimental inaccuracies. They are considered to be correlative with the Calmer basalts [Strong et al., 1978b]. They occur on the beach east and west of Famine Back Cove, with an exposed thickness of 15 m. They were sampled through their thickness over a distance of 1 km. The magnetization of three cores is univectorial (Figures 5 and 6). It remains little changed in alternating fields up to 100 mT and temperatures up to 650øC, and it points to the southeast with intermediate downward inclination. The basalts have un- dergone intense deuteric alteration and hematite is the main carrier of the magnetization. In nine cores there is also a substantial (PEF) component, aligned close to the present earth's field, that is removed at low temperatures or after treatment in low alternating fields. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. The remaining three cores have not only PEF and SE magnetizations, but also very small magnetizations sometimes pointing south sometimes north. These very small components could not be accurately isolated (Figure 7). The northerly ones could be overprints acquired at the time of intrusion of the St. Lawrence Granite (see

d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. . IRVING AND D. F. STRONG Pacific Geoscience Centre, Sidney, British Columbia, Canada Department of Earth Sciences, Memorial University, St. John's, Newfoundland, Canada The posttectonic St. Lawrence Granite (360 + 5 Ma) and associated subvertical dikes have two mag- netizations, N and H. N points north with an intermediate upward inclination (declination, 005 ø' incli- nation, -50 ø' alpha (95), 10 ø' paleopole 12øN, 120øE). We consider N to have been acquired close to the time of initial cooling. The H magnetization points south with low inclination. H is also the dominant magnetization in the nearby Permo-Carboniferous Spanish Room Formation. H is considered to be an overprint acquired chemically during the Kiaman Reversed Superchron (Late Carboniferous and Per- mian). The N magnetization corresponds to a paleolatitude of 31 + 7øS, very different from the near- equatorial values expected from the commonly accepted Late Devonian and earliest Carboniferous (Tournaisian) reference paleofields for cratonic North America. This is generally consistent with the hypothesis of a southerly displaced Acadia proposed by Kent and Opdyke, although the displacement is much greater (30 ø rather than 15ø). However, we show that all inclinations observed from Middle to Upper Devonian and T

dies show small departures of only a few degrees (with one exception based on limited sampling and two from the Colorado Plateau which may have been rotated) which could be caused by experimental inaccuracies. Moreover the directions obtained from cratonic studies are 97% reversed, as they are in rocks with Kiaman magnetizations. We suggest, therefore, that the commonly accepted Late Devonian to earliest Carboniferous reference paleofield for North America is either entirely Kiaman in age or has been seriously affected by Kiaman overprinting. Consequently, the 30 ø of southerly displacement which the N magnetization of the St. Lawrence Granite apears to indicate, and the 15 ø invoked by Kent and Opdyke, we consider to be illusory. Three Late Precambrian rock units (623 to 606 Ma) have scattered declinations but similar inclinations yielding paleolatitudes of about 35 ø. The scattered declinations presumable were caused by local pre- Carboniferous relative rotations. There is little or no evidence of Kiaman overprinting in Precambrian rocks, indicating that overprinting is comparatively superficial and is probably related to Late Paleozoic groundwater circulation. INTRODUCTION The main purpose of this paper is to describe new paleo- magnetic results from the Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous St. Lawrence Granite of the Avalon Zone of eastern New- foundland, and to compare them with results from rocks of comparable age from cratonic North America in order to de- termine if there has been any motion between the Avalon Zone and the craton. The Avalon Zone, of which the Burin Peninsula is part, extends intermittently from Newfoundland to Florida. Its rock sequences have been compared to similar sequences of North Africa and western Europe [Schenk, 1971; Rast et al., 1976; Strong, 1978], and it could therefore be a fragment of the eastern continents left behind by the Mesozoic opening of the Atlantic [Wilson, 1966]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. Received 1985 November 4; in original form 1985 April 19 Summary. A palaeomagnetic study of the Moulin de Chateaupanne formation reveals two characteristic components of magnetization. The first one, isolated by thermal treatment at intermediate temperatures, is strongly resistant to chemical leaching. Its direction (D= 217", I= +25", ag5 = 5.5) and the corresponding pole position (Lat = 21"S, Long = 320"E) are typical of the Hercynian overprints in the Armorican Massif. The second component, carried by fine-grained haematite, presents a steep downward direction (D = 228", I = + 81", ag5 = 6" ; pole position Lat = 34"N, Long = 343"E) already recognized in other Ordovician rock units from the same area. It is resistant to high-temperature demagnetization treatment and is believed to be of chemical origin, as assessed by a conglomerate test. A mutual consistency test with the nearby Thouars Massif suggests that the tilt of the formation has a sedimentary origin, and that the Thouars Massif has not suffered significant tilt during the Hercynian orogenic events. The results are displayed in Fig. 6 and it appears that the pebble magnetization is not random. On the contrary it presents a trend towards the matrix magnetization direction. We therefore propose that the acquisition of magnetization in the matrix is younger than the sedimentation of the pebbles and we assign a post-depositional (chemical) origin to the matrix magnetization, carried in large part by the fine-grained haematite pigment. Multicomponent magnetizations of the Snowy River Volcanics have been resolved into pre-folding (dec. = 340.1', inc.= -59.2') and post-folding (dec. = 10.5', inc. = -72.3") elements. The former is attributed to initial cooling of the volcanics while the latter is probably related to the waning stages of the deformational episode which was presumably accompanied by cooling. We argue that the pole position from the pre-folding magnetizations (lat. = 74.3"S, long, = 222.7"E) represents the Australian palaeopole for the early Devonian. A reassessment of other Australian pole positions determined from rocks of about this age suggests that remagnetization during the Carboniferous may be common. Interpretation of the pole path prior to the Devonian is equivocal and awaits further study. The post-folding magnetizations from the volcanics are similar in stability and direction to those from the Buchan Caves Limestone (dec. = 27.8', inc. = - 75.6"), which appears to be completely remagnetized. The former is attributed to initial cooling of the volcanics while the latter is probably related to the waning stages of the deformational episode which was presumably accompanied by cooling. We argue that the pole position from the pre-folding magnetizations (lat. = 74.3"S, long, = 222.7"E) represents the Australian palaeopole for the early Devonian. A reassessment of other Australian pole positions determined from rocks of about this age suggests that remagnetization during the Carboniferous may be common. Interpretation of the pole path prior to the Devonian is equivocal and awaits further study. Ireland north of the proposed suture (e.g. Phillips et af. 1976) is one area where previous Ordovician palaeomagnetic work led to conflicting interpretations. le that other palaeomagnetic signatures observed in that region are the result of tectonic distortion. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. Its western margin has been reworked by tectono-orogenic processes of the Andean chain. The northern

astern part of the South American platform at the end of the Brasiliano cycle: in Paranil State, the Castro Group covers an area of about 900 km2 (Trein & Fuck 1967) with intercalating sedimentary and volcanic (acid to intermediate) sequences which have been dated by RbISr at 365 366 M. S. D'Agrella-Filho and I. G. Pacca 425Ma (Cordani, Halpern & Berenholc 1974). In Santa Catarina State, volcano-sedimentary sequences are found in the Corup6 Graben and in the Campo Alegre and Itajai Basins and they have been called the Itajd Group by Schulz Jr., Albuquerque & Giffoni (1969), who subdivided it, from youngest to oldest, into the Bau Formation which is composed of lithified conglomerates, the Campo Alegre Formation which is composed of rhyolite flows and dykes and tuff sediments and the Garcia Formation which comprises siltstones, sandstones, shales and conglomerate sandstones. Several datings have been effected for the ItajaI Group units, such as K/Ar dates of 430 and 460Ma (Ebert 1971) and a Rb/Sr date of 585Ma (Teixeira 1982) for the Campo Alegre acid lavas. Volcano-sedimentary sequences of similar age outcrop also in the State of Rio Grande do Sul. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. Key words: Brasiliano cycle, palaeomagnetic poles, APW path, Gondwana 1 INTRODUCTION The South American platform comprises most of the South African continent. Its western margin has been reworked by tectono-orogenic processes of the Andean chain. The northern

astern part of the South American platform at the end of the Brasiliano cycle: in Paranil State, the Castro Group covers an area of about 900 km2 (Trein & Fuck 1967) with intercalating sedimentary and volcanic (acid to intermediate) sequences which have been dated by RbISr at 365 366 M. S. D'Agrella-Filho and I. G. Pacca 425Ma (Cordani, Halpern & Berenholc 1974). In Santa Catarina State, volcano-sedimentary sequences are found in the Corup6 Graben and in the Campo Alegre and Itajai Basins and they have been called the Itajd Group by Schulz Jr., Albuquerque & Giffoni (1969), who subdivided it, from youngest to oldest, into the Bau Formation which is composed of lithified conglomerates, the Campo Alegre Formation which is composed of rhyolite flows and dykes and tuff sediments and the Garcia Formation which comprises siltstones, sandstones, shales and conglomerate sandstones. Several datings have been effected for the ItajaI Group units, such as K/Ar dates of 430 and 460Ma (Ebert 1971) and a Rb/Sr date of 585Ma (Teixeira 1982) for the Campo Alegre acid lavas. Volcano-sedimentary sequences of similar age outcrop also in the State of Rio Grande do Sul. Magnetite is optically observed to occur in three common forms namely, (i) large skeletal grains, (ii) fine dusts and clusters of small grains in association with serpentine alteration products after olivine and pyroxene, and (iii) as irregular trains of crystals in serpentine veins which cross-cut each other and all earlier fabrics. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. boniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. Such alteration events are likely to have been due to either tectonic or climatic processes, for example Devonian strike-slip motions or permo- Carboniferous weathering regimes. The complex consists essentially of two ophiolitic thrust nappes separated from each other and the underlying basement rocks by melanges of both tectonic and sedimentary origin (Fig. 1). The basement to the area comprises heterogeneous schists and gneisses which have been equated with the Lower Dalradian Succession of Scotland (Flinn et al. 1972). This basement is overlain by thrust sheets composed of metasediments (the Saxa Vord block of Fig. 1) which have been interpreted (Flinn 1958) as being emplaced prior to the ophiolite complex thrust sheets. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. This basement is overlain by thrust sheets composed of metasediments (the Saxa Vord block of Fig. 1) which have been interpreted (Flinn 1958) as being emplaced prior to the ophiolite complex thrust sheets. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. Many of these units are banded or layered both at the main lithological boundaries and internally. In addition dolerite dykes, plagigranites and metavolcanics have all been recorded from the lower thrust nappe to provide a complete representation of all the members of a normal ophiolite sequence. The upper ophiolitic thrust nappe consists predominantly of harzburgite, with occasional lenses of dunite, which is commonly found to be banded or layered. No simple structural model has yet emerged for the complex as a whole. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. The complex consists essentially of two ophiolitic thrust nappes separated from each other and the underlying basement rocks by melanges of both tectonic and sedimentary origin (Fig. 1). The basement to the area comprises heterogeneous schists and gneisses which have been equated with the Lower Dalradian Succession of Scotland (Flinn et al. 1972). This basement is overlain by thrust sheets composed of metasediments (the Saxa Vord block of Fig. 1) which have been interpreted (Flinn 1958) as being emplaced prior to the ophiolite complex thrust sheets. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. Many of these units are banded or layered both at the main lithological boundaries and internally. All of these rocks have suffered late stage greenschist metamorphism which has produced chlorite as the dominant -Fe-bearing phase; this metamorphism may have been responsible for the alteration of any original magnetite present. In contrast, the serpentinised ultra- mafites tend to have large NRM intensities, often in excess of 1Am-1, and high bulk susceptibilities reflecting the relatively high modal content (1-5 per cent) of magnetite in these rocks. Magnetite is optically observed to occur in three common forms namely, (i) large skeletal grains, (ii) fine dusts and clusters of small grains in association with serpentine alteration products after olivine and pyroxene, and (iii) as irregular trains of crystals in serpentine veins which cross-cut each other and all earlier fabrics. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. boniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. Such alteration events are likely to have been due to either tectonic or climatic processes, for example Devonian strike-slip motions or permo- Carboniferous weathering regimes. In granitic rocks, DIRM has been found to have coercivities primarily <15 mT, to affect coarse-grained rocks more than fine-grained ones, and to reside mainly in magnetic grains close to the cutting surface (Burmester 1977; Kodama 1984). In these respects, the soft NRM of our cores resembles DIRM (Figs 4,5,7). Jackson & Van der Voo (1985) concluded from a careful study of carbonate rocks that magnetites as fine as 1-2pm in size acquire drilling and sawing remanences, which resist demagnetization to 60 mT or 400°C. DIRM in our samples was erased by 20mT OT 400°C cleaning and presumably resides in much coarser magnetites. The mechanism of DIRM remains in doubt. Burmester (1977) found that DIRM had a logt time decay, in the manner of VRM, but only a small part of DIRM intensity could be accounted for by VRM acquired in the axial core-barrel field of -0.2rnT during a period of several weeks. Storage of our samples in the laboratory field of 60pT for six weeks resulted in negligible VRM. For a drilling rate of =lft hr-' in crystalline rock, our samples, which came from the deepest section cored, would have been exposed to the core-barrel field for only about one day. Before dismissing VRM as a principal mechanism of DIRM, we should consider the possible role of elevated temperatures in amplifying VRM. In this interpretation, the soft NRM would itself be a bivectorial combination of a steep VRM and a vertical DIRM, whose directions are not resolved in vector diagrams like Fig. 7(c). Vector swings from 0 to 2 mT AF cleaning often do have an easterly swing away from vertical at odds with the generally southerly vector swings at higher AFs (e.g. Fig. 7a), but many of the soft vectors lie far from the N-S vertical plane which would be expected to contain such composite vectors. Whatever the origin of the soft NRM vector, it plays an important role in deducing the declination and even the polarity of stable NRM in unoriented cores (Ade-Hall & Johnson 1976; Kodama, 1984). From Fig. 8(b), it is obvious that in the present study declinations of individual soft NRMs are widely scattered. They would be a poor guide to present geographic or geomagnetic north for individual specimens; the multishot orientation technique is more trustworthy in the case of our core. The exact extent of the 1900-1700Ma path (the Coronation Loop of Irving & McGlynn 1979) is uncertain, but its general trend is well established. The main group of 20 cleaned hard NRMs give a VGP at 4"S, 93"W (dp = 3", dm =4"), falling on the APWP around 1850Ma. Even allowing for PSV, the age of magnetization is likely between 1900 and 1800 Ma. Uplift and cooling overprint magnetizations from the Churchill, Superior and North Atlantic cratons tend to fall on the ascending limb of the Coronation Loop, between 1750 and 1650Ma. Key words: Churchill Province, oriented drillcore, palaeomagnetism, Proterozoic basement 1 INTRODUCTION Because of the importance of testing the Vine & Matthews' (1963) hypothesis, there has been lively interest in the paleomagnetism of igneous basement cores drilled in the Deep Sea Drilling Project (DSDP). Since DSDP cores are unoriented in azimuth, only the inclination of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) can be determined. There have been comparatively few paleomagnetic studies of continental sedimentary sections and igneous basement sampled by boreholes (Van der Voo & Watts 1978; Kodama 1984; Evans & Maillol 1986). There have been comparatively few paleomagnetic studies of continental sedimentary sections and igneous basement sampled by boreholes (Van der Voo & Watts 1978; Kodama 1984; Evans & Maillol 1986). In most cases, azimuthal orientation of the cores and NRM declinations were determined indirectly, using sedimentary fabric or secondary magnetization directions. The drillcore studied in this paper (PCP Travers 1-31-13-2OW4) was fully oriented by the Christensen-Huge1 method. It was drilled by the PanCanadian Petroleum Company through a 2531 m sedimentary section in southern Alberta (5O.l0N, 112.7"W). Underlying the basal Cambrian sandstone and a weathered interval at the unconformity was fresh unweathered granodiorite, which was cored from 2550 to 2563 m. A 7 m section from the base of this igneous core is studied here. Since the drillhole is located several hundred km east of the Foothills Thrust Belt, tectonic rotation of the granodiorite pluton is unlikely and we have made no tilt corrections to the data that follow. This part of the basement of Alberta is thought to belong to the Churchill Structural Province of the Canadian Precambrian Shield (Fig. 1).
